name: Saab
overview: Quirky, aerospace-inspired Swedish carmaker celebrated in Australia for turbocharging leadership, wraparound windscreens, and ignition keys between the front seats.
australian_history: Saab entered Australia in the early 1960s with the two-stroke 96 and V4. The brand gained a passionate following among Australian architects, academics, and doctors with the launch of the 99 Turbo in 1978 and the iconic 900. The classic Saab 900 Turbo and 900 Convertible became status symbols in Sydney and Melbourne through the 1980s. General Motors acquired a 50% stake in 1989 and full ownership in 2000, integrating Saab distribution into GM-Holden's network. Following GM's bankruptcy and Spyker's brief ownership, Saab ceased vehicle production globally in late 2011, and Saab Australia wound up operations in 2012.

models.overview: Born from jets. Saab brought Swedish aircraft engineering, wraparound windscreens, night panels, and turbocharging mastery to Australia across more than three decades. The Classic 900 Turbo established Saab's intellectual cool, followed by the lightning-quick 9-3 Viggen and the 206kW 2.8T Aero V6.
The definitive classic Saab, featuring aircraft cockpit ergonomics, front-hinged clamshell bonnet, and punchy turbo power.
Successor to the 900, offered in Linear, Arc, Vector, Aero, and rare all-wheel drive Turbo X.

900-9-3.australian_market_notes: First sold in Australia in 1979 (Classic 900). The 900 Turbo Cabriolet became an icon of Australian coastal affluence and design distinction. The 9-3 Viggen—named after the Saab 37 Viggen fighter aircraft—became a rare Australian cult vehicle with 169kW through the front wheels.
